"EME" stands for "Encrypted Media Extension" and is now a new addition to the HTML5 standard meant for "Digital Rights Management", namely by sending media-content in an encrypted format to the client and only decrypting it for direct playback in the browser, meaning that the browser has to provide an interface for proprietary decryption algorithms.

An example would be "Widevine", a Google project, and the way it is currently used in Mozilla Firefox, including the proprietary module that is downloaded the first time the user tries to play according content.

The reasons why it faces criticism are likely as follows - Firstly, making this part of the standard implies that every browser should now offer that feature, or no longer be compliant; Secondly, it is possible that the proprietary modules do more than just decrypt content, like report back what content is played and when on which exact device etc.;

For reference: https://www.w3.org/TR/encrypted-media/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encrypted_Media_Extensions

This is better than my evaluation, I think the main nuance I had is that it also allows [and encourages] browsers to document tampering of copyrighted materials, if one attempts to do so.

Also, it is a threat on open source software. If the decryption algorithm is not made available to the public, then the concept of open source browsers is heavily reduced. If the decryption algorithm is public, then it re-inforces that reverse engineering it is a legal offense.
